newsitem.title: UK: Scandinavian bonds take the lead in week -Salomon.
newsitem.headline: Scandinavian bonds take the lead in week -Salomon.

text.p: Scandinavian bonds led the field in the latest week, with Sweden and Finland outpacing other main government bonds, according to the Salomon Brothers world government bond index released on Friday.
All the countries represented made gains during the week and the index as a whole gained 0.56 percent in local currency terms but fell 0.49 percent in U.S. dollar terms.
Swedish bonds topped the bill as the market gained support from low inflation signals and the Riksbank cut its key repo rate for the 19th time this year.

The index showed Sweden gained 1.13 percent in local currency terms and 0.46 percent in terms of U.S. dollars. Finnish debt increased 0.95 percent in local currency terms, but fell 0.50 percent in dollar terms.
JGBs were the losers this week, lagging other debt markets with gains of only 0.39 percent in local currency terms and a loss of 0.40 percent in dollar terms.
Gilts were only slightly ahead of JGBs, gaining 0.43 percent in local currency terms and falling 0.37 percent in dollars.

In the core European countries, France showed local currency gains of 0.64 percent but a 0.87 percent deficit in dollar terms, while German debt gained 0.51 percent in local currency terms and fell 1.31 percent in dollar terms.
Italian bonds were slightly more successful, gaining 0.77 percent in lira terms.
U.S. Treasuries performed modestly during the week showing gains of 0.56 percent, the same as the index itself.
Outside Salomon's main world index, New Zealand bonds showed the strongest gains of the week coming in at 1.26 percent in local currency terms and 0.57 percent in U.S. dollar terms.

Salomon's bond index is calculated using all government bonds with over one year to maturity, weighted for market capitalisation. Only bonds freely available to institutional investors and with a certain minimum amount outstanding are included. Returns take account of price moves and accrued interest.
